question:
For a project I am working I want to implement a small prototype to try things out, demonstrate some functionality to the client and learn some frameworks used in the project.

Do you have any suggestions or do you know of best practices for implementing such a prototype?

Some more details:

The application will be a complex web app

I have to implement a mechanism where the server pushes data to subscribed clients (the data will be generated by some events)

I want to write a prototype which implements exactly this behaviour but nothing more
answer_raw:
For a focused prototype like this, the golden rule is to avoid over-engineering. Since you only need server-to-client pushes, don't waste time on complex authentication or a full database; use mock data and hardcoded IDs. For the tech stack, I'd recommend WebSockets via Socket.io or Server-Sent Events (SSE), depending on whether you need bidirectional communication. SSE is often simpler if you only need one-way pushes.

To simulate the events, a simple Redis Pub/Sub setup is ideal because it decouples the event trigger from the delivery mechanism, mimicking how a real complex app would actually function. Keep your frontend minimal—just a simple list that updates in real-time. This allows you to isolate the networking logic and framework learning without getting bogged down in UI polish. Focus on the "happy path" first, and only add robust error handling once the core push mechanism is proven to your client.

question:
I understand the difference between the two, but I get questioned by my colleagues of the benefit of labeling requirements as functional or nonfunctional (or transitional). Why bother to do so? He spent what he said was two days going through a list of requirements for one project, and saw no benefit to it, because the end result was to submit the document to another business entity with the edict, "Do it all."

What I fear is requirements lumped together in one document. I tried to explain the benefit in practical terms, but couldn't sell it. How do I sell the benefit of documenting which requirements are functional and which are nonfunctional.
answer_raw:
The problem with a "do it all" approach is that it obscures systemic risk. Functional requirements define *what* the system does, but non-functional requirements (NFRs) define *how* it performs. If you lump them together, you risk delivering a product that executes every feature perfectly but crashes under load or fails a security audit because those constraints weren't prioritized as architectural drivers.

Practically, labeling dictates how you validate the project. You test a functional requirement with a user story, but you validate an NFR with a stress test or a penetration audit. Furthermore, NFRs often dictate the entire tech stack and infrastructure. If developers treat a performance requirement as just another "feature" in a long list, they may overlook the fundamental architectural changes needed to support it. Labeling isn't about bookkeeping; it’s about ensuring the system is actually viable and sustainable in a production environment.

question:
I have a very small and basic web site on a web server. Usually I'm doing the changes on a localhost where the development version is, and after that I upload it to the server with FileZilla. That's the very obvious way, but it's not the most convenient.

I've worked with SVN, but I've never needed to set anything - just checkout, commit, update. Reading some tutorials I wonder is this the easier way to upload the files to a server? Or are there any easier?
answer_raw:
SVN is a bit outdated; these days, Git is the industry standard. Instead of manually dragging files in FileZilla, you should look into a Git-based workflow. The most common approach is to push your code to a repository like GitHub or GitLab and then use a CI/CD tool, such as GitHub Actions, to automatically deploy those changes to your server whenever you push a commit.

If a full automation pipeline feels like overkill for a basic site, try an IDE extension. If you use VS Code, there are "SFTP" plugins that allow you to sync files to your server instantly upon saving, effectively automating FileZilla in the background. For those comfortable with the command line, Rsync is another powerful alternative for syncing only changed files. Ultimately, learning Git is the best move; it provides a safety net via version control and opens the door to professional deployment workflows.

question:
MVC is pretty straightforward. There is a Model, a Controller and a View. When we create a website, it all come together as 'client sends REST keyword request to server -> the server matches the requested URL to the controller action -> which then calls the model(s) for data gathering/processing, gets the result -> and returns the result back to the client as a HTML page (view)'.

What if we are talking about a pure RESTful API web service? Then the flow with be something like 'client sends REST keyword request to server -> the server matches the requested URL to the controller action -> which then calls the model(s) for data gathering/processing, gets the result -> and returns the result back to the client in JSON'. Same as before, but there is no 'view'...or rather, the generated JSON can be thought of as a 'view'. In a sense, we are only utilizing the MC part of MVC. Is that how it is should be done? Or are there any other, better-suited patterns for a API-only service instead of MVC?
answer_raw:
You're essentially correct. In a RESTful API, the JSON response is functionally the "View." The View layer hasn't disappeared; it has simply shifted from an HTML template engine to a data serializer. The goal remains the same: presenting the model's data in a format the client can consume.

However, for professional API services, most developers move beyond basic MVC toward Layered Architecture or Clean Architecture. Instead of just "Controller" and "Model," you introduce a Service Layer for business logic and a Repository Layer for data access. This prevents the "Fat Controller" problem, where controllers end up handling too much heavy lifting and become difficult to test.

So, while you're still conceptually following the MVC flow, the internal structure becomes more granular. You aren't just using "MC"; you're using a decoupled stack where the JSON serialization is the final, lightweight step of the View process.

question:
I migrated some files from one Version Control System to another. I have to prove that content are identical (between source and destination, denote 1 , 2). There are a few zips files (lets call them A B C) each of which contains hundreds of files. I am looking at best way to do CRC comparison between content in old VCS against the new one.

1) Generate CRC on each ZIP file as a whole and compare the CRC of 2 corresponding zips file. ZIP-ZIP CRC comparison.

Obviously, this approach will be easier. But I don't know what will include in calculation of CRC. Or even if CRC of two zip files with identical file content might be different.(modified date?).

2) Compare CRC of each files in zip against corresponding files. File-File CRC Comparison

with this approach, I will have to write a script that goes through each file in zip (say A1) and extract their CRC. Build a list with [path file name, crc]. do the same for zip(A2). Compare list.

Have anyone ever done something like this?
answer_raw:
Avoid the ZIP-to-ZIP approach. Even if the internal contents are identical, the ZIP binary itself can differ due to metadata like timestamps, compression levels, or the order in which files were added. This would give you a false negative.

The file-by-file approach is the only way to truly prove content integrity. The most efficient method is to unzip both versions into separate temporary directories and generate a checksum manifest for every file. On Linux or macOS, you can use a command like `find . -type f -exec sha256sum {} + | sort > manifest.txt`. 

Run this for both the source and destination directories, then use `diff` to compare the two manifest files. This provides a definitive audit trail and ensures that every single file is identical regardless of how the archive was packaged. It is a standard industry practice for verifying large-scale migrations.

question: When considering what Windows event logs to incorporate into a SIEM solution, should I be looking at just the Security event logs, or all categories of event log? How useful are the other categories in detecting and responding to security incidents?
answer_raw:
You definitely shouldn't stop at just the Security logs. While the Security log is the foundation for tracking logins and privilege escalations, relying on it alone leaves massive blind spots. The System log is essential because it records when critical services are stopped or when unexpected reboots occur—often signs of an attacker disabling security software or exploiting a kernel vulnerability. Application logs can similarly reveal crashes or errors that signal a failed exploit attempt.

Furthermore, for a professional setup, you should prioritize Sysmon and PowerShell logs. Sysmon provides the process-level granularity, such as network connections and file creation, that standard Windows logs lack. Security incidents rarely happen in a vacuum; by collecting System and Application logs alongside Security, you gain the necessary context to reconstruct an attack chain and differentiate a technical glitch from a targeted breach. Stick to a risk-based approach, but broaden your scope.

question:
For a few years i stored my personal text files encrypted using an asymmetric key through GnuPG. Now i thought that it is a good idea to also encrypt my hard drive partition. Does it make sense to use both filesystem encryption (via, say, dm-crypt) and encryption via GPG for separate files? If this is unnecessary, what should i stick with for personal encryption of textual data?

I want to be able to use version control system and text processing tools on these files and also optionally apply steganography to conceal the existence of the files from intruders altogether.

I use GNU/Linux.
answer_raw:
Yes, it makes sense to use both. This approach, known as defense in depth, protects you at different threat levels. Disk encryption via dm-crypt protects your data if the physical hardware is stolen, but once you've booted into your session and mounted the drive, the files are transparently available. GPG adds a second layer; if an attacker gains remote access to your running system, they still cannot read GPG-encrypted files without your private key.

For version control and text processing, disk encryption is the winner. It allows you to use tools like Git and Vim natively on your files without the friction of constant decryption cycles. However, for steganography, GPG is essential. You cannot hide a partition easily, but you can embed a GPG-encrypted binary blob inside an image or audio file to conceal its existence entirely. Use dm-crypt for your daily workflow and GPG for your most sensitive secrets.

question:
I'd like to know if Aescrypt is a valid tool, or if for a very secure protection, the only choice is to use a software like gpg, or similar.

More I've another curiosity, if one doesn't want to use encrypted email with a related software, could it be secure send AES encrypted files, through normal email connection ? Could it be usefull to use a rar AES protected archive, to further protect files ?

Thanks
answer_raw:
AESCrypt is a perfectly valid tool. It uses AES-256, the industry standard for symmetric encryption. While GPG is more versatile because it uses public-key cryptography—allowing you to send files without sharing a password beforehand—AESCrypt is excellent for simple, straightforward file protection.

Sending AES-encrypted files via standard email is secure, provided you do not send the decryption password in the same email or thread. The file remains encrypted regardless of the email provider's security or the transport protocol used.

Regarding RAR, using an AES-protected archive is a great alternative to standalone tools. It allows you to bundle multiple files and encrypt them simultaneously. Layering a RAR archive inside another encrypted file is generally unnecessary "security theater" and offers little additional benefit, but using a RAR archive as your primary encryption method is a solid, practical choice. Just ensure you use a long, complex password.

question:
For the purpose of a forensic mission, we must get a docker image without using the famous export from a docker command.

Does copy and paste of the folder /var/lib/docker/containers in another server allow us to retrieve information without any corrupted data?

Thanks.
answer_raw:
No, copying only `/var/lib/docker/containers` is insufficient. That directory primarily contains configuration files, host IDs, and logs, not the actual filesystem of the container. The actual data and image layers reside in `/var/lib/docker/overlay2` (on most modern Linux distributions). To reconstruct the environment, you would need both directories and the associated metadata.

Regarding corruption, copying files from a live, running system is highly risky. Because Docker is constantly writing to these directories, you risk capturing a partial state, which leads to inconsistent files or corrupted databases. For a forensic mission, this is generally unacceptable. Your best approach is to take a full snapshot of the host machine's disk or stop the Docker daemon entirely before copying the entire `/var/lib/docker` directory. This ensures a consistent state and prevents data corruption during the transfer process.

question:
The use of paid API is increasingly rising each year. For example, IBM, Google and Microsoft are providing paid API such as Text to Speech, Speech to Text and Image to Text and vice versa.

I have a question about what happens If I build an app and publish it:

1.What happens when another person use Wireshack or reverse engineering to obtain the key of this API and then use it in their app or sell it?

2.Will I be paying for this even though my clients are not the people using this API?

3.Is there a way to reduce or prevent this from happening?

I am just worried about this and sure this is happening or must have happened at some point.

NOTE:

I asked this because I saw my Google Map API with the Wireshark software.

My initial solution is to make each user create username and password and apply restrictions to each individual user but those companies I mentioned up don't do that. They simply use one single key for their services.
answer_raw:
If you embed an API key directly in your frontend code, it is effectively public. Anyone using a packet sniffer like Wireshark or a decompiler can steal it. Since providers bill the account associated with the key, you will be responsible for all costs incurred by the thief, even if they sell the access to others.

To prevent this, never call paid APIs directly from the client side. Instead, implement a backend proxy. Your app should send requests to your own server, which then forwards the request to the API provider using a key stored securely in environment variables. This allows you to manage authentication, implement rate limiting, and monitor usage. For specific services that require client-side keys, such as Google Maps, use the provider's restriction settings to limit the key's validity to your specific domain or app ID, rendering a stolen key useless on other platforms.

question: I know the difference between clustering and classification in machine learning, but I don't understand the difference between text classification and topic modeling for documents. Can I use topic modeling over documents to identify a topic? Can I use classification methods to classify the text inside these documents?
answer_raw:
Text classification is a supervised learning task. You start with predefined labels—like "Sports" or "Politics"—and train a model to assign new text to those specific categories. If you have a labeled dataset, this is exactly how you categorize the text inside your documents.

Topic modeling, however, is unsupervised. It doesn't use labels; instead, it discovers hidden patterns by grouping words that frequently appear together. You can absolutely use it to identify topics, but the model won't give you a human-readable name. It will provide a cluster of words—for example, "court, judge, law"—and you, the human, must interpret that as the "Legal" topic.

In short, use classification when you already know what categories you are looking for, and use topic modeling when you want the data to reveal which themes exist without making any prior assumptions.

question:
Is it correct to say that any statistical learning algorithm (linear/logistic regression, SVM, neural network, random forest) can be implemented inside a Map Reduce framework? Or are there restrictions?

I guess there may be some algorithms that is not possible to parallelize?
answer_raw:
Technically, yes, you can implement almost any statistical learning algorithm in MapReduce, but there is a massive difference between "possible" and "practical." MapReduce is designed for batch processing, which creates significant friction for iterative algorithms. For example, Logistic Regression and Neural Networks rely on gradient descent, requiring many passes over the data. In a standard MapReduce framework, each iteration requires writing to and reading from disk, creating a crippling I/O bottleneck.

Conversely, "embarrassingly parallel" algorithms, such as Random Forests where individual trees can be trained independently, fit the framework perfectly. The primary restriction is the lack of a shared memory state. If an algorithm is strictly sequential—where step N depends entirely on the global result of step N-1—parallelization becomes inefficient. This is precisely why the industry shifted toward frameworks like Apache Spark, which maintains data in memory rather than relying on the rigid, disk-heavy Map-Shuffle-Reduce cycle.

question:
I was posting on stats.stackexchange but perhaps I should be posting here.

Context. Subscription business that charges users a monthly fee for access to the service. Management would like to predict "churn" - subscriptions who are likely to cancel. Management would like to create an email sequence in attempt to prevent high risk accounts from churning, perhaps with a discount code of some sort. So I need to identify those accounts at risk of leaving us.

I have a dataset with say 50k records. Each line item is an account number along with some variables. One of the variables is "Churned" with a value of "yes" (they cancelled) or "No" (they are active).

The dataset I have is all data since the beginning of time for the business. About 20k records are active paying customers and about 30k are those who used to be paying customers but who have since cancelled.

My task is to build a model to predict which of the 20k active customers are currently likely to churn.

Here is where I have tied my brain in a knott. I need to run the model (Predict) on the 20k records of active customers.

How do I split my data between training, test and predict?

Does predict data have to be exclusive of train and test data?

Can I split the entire dataset of 50k into 0.8 train and 0.2 test, build a model and then predict on the 20k active accounts? That would imply I'm training and testing on data that I'm also going to predict on. Seems "wrong". Is it?
answer_raw:
You are confusing model validation with model deployment. Training and testing are used to ensure your model actually works; prediction is the act of applying that finished model to solve the business problem.

It is standard practice to split your entire 50k dataset (e.g., 80/20) to train and validate the model. This process allows you to measure accuracy using the test set. Once you are satisfied with the performance, you then run the model on your 20k active customers to identify who is at risk.

Predicting on users who were part of the training set isn't "wrong" for business purposes, but it can be slightly biased because the model has already seen those records. However, since you need "No" examples to teach the model what a loyal customer looks like, you must include active users in your training data. The test set is for measuring performance, while the 20k active users are your target for action.

question: As I was checking the /etc/fstab I noticed that the swap space has attr pass=0, which means its filesystem is not checked at boot time. Can anyone please tell me why is this behavior for?
answer_raw:
The `pass` field in `/etc/fstab` tells the system whether `fsck` should check the partition for errors during the boot process. A value of 0 tells the system to skip the check entirely. The reason swap is set to 0 is that swap space isn't actually a filesystem. Unlike ext4 or XFS, swap doesn't store files, folders, or a directory structure; it is essentially a raw area of the disk used as an extension of your system's RAM.

Because it lacks a traditional filesystem layout, there are no inodes, superblocks, or journals for `fsck` to verify or repair. Running a filesystem check on a swap partition would be meaningless because there is no filesystem metadata to validate. If the swap area is physically corrupted, the kernel generally handles it during the activation process or ignores the bad sectors, rather than requiring a boot-time consistency check.

question: When we do k-fold cross validation, should we just use the classifier that has the highest test accuracy? What is generally the best approach in getting a classifier from cross validation?
answer_raw:
Not exactly. K-fold cross-validation isn't designed to pick a "winning" model from the folds. If you simply choose the model that performed best on one specific fold, you are essentially overfitting to that particular data split.

The standard approach is to use cross-validation for model selection or hyperparameter tuning. You use the average performance across all folds to determine which set of hyperparameters (like the depth of a decision tree) works best. Once you have identified the optimal configuration, you retrain a single final model using those specific parameters on your entire training dataset. This ensures the model leverages all available data to learn the underlying patterns. question:
Say you're building a sales prediction model to predict tomorrow's sales value, as well as the next 2 weeks of daily sales. The model is being trained using daily data for the previous 1.5 years, and it follows a strong weekly seasonality pattern.

Obviously once you are happy with model performance, would it be necessary to re-train the model everyday to capture data up to and including yesterday in order to get the most accurate prediction for tomorrow's sales value? Essentially, the model would be trained on a rolling 1.5 year data set to capture yesterday's sales value.

Or does it depend on the type of model being used? Whether you need to to completely re-train when new data is present

I can see why it would make sense to re-train your standard time series forecasting models (ARIMA etc.), but I can also understand more sophisticated models (Neural Networks etc.) may generalize well enough to not have to re-train everyday.

I am looking for an explanation of models where you would and wouldn't re-train when new time series data is present.
answer_raw:
It depends on whether the model uses new data to update its internal parameters or simply as input features. For statistical models like ARIMA or Exponential Smoothing, retraining or updating the state is essential because they rely on the most recent observations to establish the current baseline and trend. Without yesterday's data, the forecast starts from an outdated point.

Conversely, machine learning models like LSTMs or XGBoost typically treat recent history as "lagged features." As long as the model has learned the general seasonal patterns and relationships, you only need to feed yesterday's sales into the input vector rather than updating the model weights. You would only retrain these periodically—perhaps monthly—to account for "concept drift," where consumer behavior changes fundamentally over time. In short: traditional statistical models generally require updating the formula, while ML models usually just require updating the inputs to generate a new prediction.

question:
When i installed ubuntu in my x86 machine, I had to configure some memory as 'swap area'.

What is the use of this memory and what is the importance of this memory in linux file systems?

How can I determine the exact size of 'swap area' in a machine for the safe working of linux inside in it?
answer_raw:
Swap acts as a virtual extension of your physical RAM. When your system runs out of actual memory, the Linux kernel moves inactive pages of data from the RAM to this dedicated area on your disk. This prevents the system from crashing or forcefully killing active applications when memory usage spikes, acting as a critical safety net for system stability.

Regarding size, there isn't a single "perfect" number, as it depends on your total RAM and specific usage. A common guideline is to set swap to twice your RAM size if you have less than 8GB. For machines with more RAM, a smaller allocation—typically 4GB to 8GB—is often sufficient for general stability. However, if you intend to use the hibernation feature, your swap area must be at least equal to your total physical RAM to save the entire system state. You can check your current setup by running `free -h` or `swapon --show` in the terminal.

question: I am changing my current partition scheme (personal development laptop, dual boot) to remove the Windows partition and leave only my Slackware64 instance. What thought should go into my partitioning? I have been keeping / and /home in separate partitions, as well as a swap partition too. How do I decide what other partitions would be good to have in their own section of the disk?
answer_raw:
Since you're already splitting `/` and `/home`, you've got the basics covered. For a development machine, the biggest risk is `/var` filling up with logs, caches, or Docker images, which can crash your system if it shares space with root. Moving `/var` to its own partition provides an extra layer of safety and prevents a runaway log file from freezing your OS. 

You might also consider a separate `/tmp` partition or moving it to RAM via tmpfs to reduce SSD wear and increase speed. If you aren't already using LVM, now is the perfect time to switch; it allows you to resize volumes on the fly without the headache of shifting physical partition boundaries. Lastly, ensure your `/boot` is properly sized for a few kernel versions. Unless you have a specific need for a dedicated encrypted vault, keeping it simple with root, home, swap, and perhaps var is usually the sweet spot for Slackware.

question:
How can I find out who executed a particular command and which terminal was used to run it?

Original:

How can I know particular cmd is executed by whom and to know about my terminal
answer_raw:
The most reliable way to track who executed a command and from which terminal is by using the Linux Audit Framework (`auditd`). If auditing is enabled, you can use `ausearch -c <command_name>` to retrieve logs containing the user ID (uid) and the terminal (tty) associated with that specific execution.

For commands run with elevated privileges, check the system authentication logs, typically located at `/var/log/auth.log` or `/var/log/secure`. These logs generally record the username and the terminal device used whenever a `sudo` command is triggered. 

If you lack these logs, you can check the `.bash_history` file in a user's home directory to see what they ran, though this won't specify the terminal. For real-time tracking, the `w` or `who` commands show who is currently logged in and their respective terminals, while `ps -ef` can link active processes back to a specific tty.

question: Why are tables built into ipchains? What was the benefit of adding tables to ipchains? Is there a simple scenario that would illustrate how tables are used to increase performance or offer some other benefit?
answer_raw:
Tables were added to ipchains to organize rules by function, moving away from a flat structure. The main benefit was a boost in performance and logical separation; it allowed the kernel to bypass entire sets of rules that weren't relevant to a packet's current state.

A great example is the distinction between NAT and filtering. If you have a massive list of security rules and a few NAT rules, you don't want every single packet to be evaluated against every security rule just to perform a simple address translation. By placing NAT rules in their own table, the system can process the translation quickly without wasting CPU cycles on the complex filtering logic. This modularity prevents the firewall from becoming a bottleneck, as the kernel only executes the specific logic required for that packet's path, significantly improving throughput under high traffic loads.

question:
I am confused by the dual concepts of time-resolution and bandwidth. Often I will hear that a pulse-compressed radar application 'doesnt have enough BW' for some specific time resolution that is sought.

Isnt the maximum time resolution simply the reciprocal of your sampling rate?

How are those concepts related?
answer_raw:
Actually, sampling rate and time resolution are distinct concepts. The sampling rate determines how accurately you can digitize a signal without aliasing, but it doesn't create resolution where none exists. Time resolution—the ability to distinguish two closely spaced targets—is fundamentally limited by the signal's bandwidth, not the digitizer.

The relationship is an inverse one: the minimum time resolution is roughly the reciprocal of the bandwidth ($\Delta t \approx 1/B$). In pulse compression, you use a wide frequency sweep (a chirp) to make a long pulse behave like a short one. If your bandwidth is too narrow, the resulting compressed pulse remains "fat" or smeared in time. No matter how fast you sample that smeared pulse, you can't magically sharpen it. You need the frequency content to create a narrow peak; without enough bandwidth, the physical limit of the signal prevents you from resolving fine details.

question: Can anyone state the difference between frequency response and impulse response in simple English?
answer_raw:
Impulse response is what happens when you give a system a single, sharp "poke"—like a quick click or a clap in a room. It shows how the system reacts over time, capturing characteristics like echoes or decay. If you record a single loud pop in a cathedral, that recording is the impulse response of that space.

Frequency response, on the other hand, describes how a system handles different pitches. Instead of a momentary burst, imagine feeding the system steady tones from low to high. The frequency response tells you if the system boosts the bass, cuts the mids, or enhances the treble.

The fundamental difference is the perspective: impulse response lives in the time domain, while frequency response lives in the frequency domain. They are essentially two sides of the same coin; if you have one, you can use a Fourier transform to mathematically calculate the other.

question:
I need help understanding how/what does it mean to "turn" a transformation parameters into a vote. I know how to recover the transformation parameters (in my case: 6 DOF), but how this turns into a vote in 6D (??) space ?

Thank You !
answer_raw:
Think of it as a Generalized Hough Transform. When you recover a transformation for a specific pair of matching features, you aren't just finding a result; you are proposing a hypothesis. This hypothesis is treated as a single coordinate in a 6D parameter space, where three dimensions represent rotation and three represent translation.

By treating this coordinate as a "vote," you are mapping each local match to a specific location in a high-dimensional histogram. If many matches are consistent with the same global motion, their corresponding transformation parameters will be nearly identical. In the 6D space, these votes will cluster tightly together. The region with the highest density of votes—the peak of the distribution—represents the most likely global transformation. Instead of relying on a single potentially noisy match, you use the consensus of all matches to find the most frequent transformation, which effectively filters out outliers and noise.

question:
I performed 512 point FFT on a signal. I got another set of 512 Numbers. I understand that those numbers represent amplitude of the various sine and cosine waves having different frequencies.

If my understanding is correct can somebody tell me how to know the frequencies of those sine and cosine waves from the knowledge of those 512-numbers (i.e amplitudes) ?
answer_raw:
To determine the frequencies, you first need to know your sampling rate ($f_s$). The FFT divides the frequency range into "bins." The distance between these bins, known as the frequency resolution, is calculated by dividing the sampling rate by the number of points in the FFT ($f_s / 512$).

Each index $k$ in your resulting array corresponds to a specific frequency: $f = k \times (f_s / 512)$. The first half of the array (indices 0 to 255) represents positive frequencies, starting from 0 Hz (the DC component) up to the Nyquist frequency, which is half of your sampling rate. For instance, if your sampling rate was 44,100 Hz, each bin would be approximately 86.1 Hz wide. The second half of the array (indices 256 to 511) represents negative frequencies, which, for real-valued input signals, are simply a mirrored reflection of the first half.

question:
I have convolved a random signal with a a Gaussian and added noise (Poisson noise in this case) to generate a noisy signal. Now I would like to deconvolve this noisy signal to extract the original signal using the same Gaussian.

The problem is that I need a code which does the job of deconvolution in 1D. (I have already found some in 2D but my main aim is 1D).

Can you please suggest me some packages or programs that are able to do so? (Preferably in MATLAB)

Thanks in advance for the help.
answer_raw:
Since you are dealing with Poisson noise, you should avoid basic inverse filtering, as it will drastically amplify high-frequency noise and ruin your signal. The gold standard for Poisson-distributed noise is the Richardson-Lucy deconvolution algorithm. In MATLAB, the Image Processing Toolbox provides a built-in function called `deconvlucy`. While typically marketed for 2D images, it works perfectly for 1D signals.

If you prefer a linear approach or find the iterative nature of Richardson-Lucy too slow, the Wiener filter is a strong alternative, implemented via `deconvwnr` in MATLAB. It balances the trade-off between signal recovery and noise suppression based on the signal-to-noise ratio. For those without the toolbox, you can manually implement Richardson-Lucy using a loop of convolutions and point-wise divisions. For more control over the smoothing, consider Tikhonov regularization, which prevents the solution from blowing up by penalizing high-frequency components.

question: I know the basic working principle of sinusoidal oscillators. But I have a doubt on this matter when I came across Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization procedure. I have read that the source for sinusoid signal output from an oscillator is the noise. Due to controlled positive feedback a single frequency component is selected and amplified, right? If the noise is a white noise, we say it has all frequency components. We think in terms of all possible sinusoids with different frequencies. When coming to frequency response too, we think in terms of sinusoids. Why can't we think in terms of other orthogonal basis set? Although it makes life difficult, I would like to know the justification for thinking in terms of sinusoids. Is sinusoids the nature's default signals?
answer_raw:
The preference for sinusoids is rooted in the fact that they are the eigenfunctions of Linear Time-Invariant (LTI) systems. Most physical oscillators are constructed from components like inductors and capacitors, which are governed by linear differential equations. In any LTI system, a sinusoid is the only waveform that can pass through the system without changing its shape; only its amplitude and phase are altered.

If you attempted to use a different orthogonal basis, such as square waves or wavelets, the system's frequency response would distort those shapes. The feedback loop essentially acts as a narrow bandpass filter, selectively amplifying the specific sinusoidal component that satisfies the Barkhausen stability criterion. Therefore, sinusoids aren't necessarily "nature's default" in a cosmic sense, but they are the inevitable mathematical result of linearity and time-invariance. When you solve the differential equations for these circuits, the solutions naturally emerge as sines and cosines.

question: What's the correct way. Should I zero-pad a signal before or after applying a windowing function?
answer_raw:
You should always apply the windowing function first, then zero-pad the result. The purpose of a window is to taper the edges of your actual sampled data to avoid spectral leakage caused by the abrupt discontinuities at the start and end of the finite signal. By applying the window to the original signal, you ensure that the transition to zero is smooth.

Once the signal is windowed, you can append zeros to reach your desired FFT length. This zero-padding doesn't add new frequency information or improve the actual resolution of your data; it simply interpolates the spectrum, giving you a smoother-looking plot and more precise peak locations in the frequency domain. If you were to zero-pad first and then apply a window of the padded length, you'd be windowing a large section of zeros, which doesn't address the leakage at the boundaries of your actual data. Stick to windowing first.

question:
When energy is referred to as the square summable sequence, is that energy a representation of the power of the signal? How is the energy of frequency determined?

E.g. what if an audio signal has high energy on the higher frequencies and another has high energy on the lower, bass, frequencies, how is this determined?

What exactly is the power from the square summable series representing then and is it useful for audio?
answer_raw:
In signal processing, energy is the sum of the squared magnitudes of a sequence. While often confused, energy is the total "amount," whereas power is the average rate over time. A square summable sequence specifically denotes a signal with finite total energy.

To determine energy across frequencies, we use the Fourier Transform. According to Parseval's Theorem, the total energy in the time domain is equal to the total energy in the frequency domain. If an audio signal is "bass-heavy," its Fourier coefficients will have larger magnitudes at lower frequencies.

This spectral energy distribution is essential for audio. It allows engineers to create equalizers, compressors, and analyzers that isolate specific bands. By calculating the power spectral density, we can identify where a signal's strength lies, which is critical for balancing a mix, removing unwanted noise, or designing crossovers for speakers to ensure the right frequencies reach the right drivers.

question: What's the difference between these? Both are measurements of some form of signal power, but surely there's some difference between the power they are measuring?
answer_raw:
The difference between dBm and dB is that one is an absolute power level while the other is a relative ratio.

dBm measures actual power relative to a fixed reference of one milliwatt (mW). When you see a value in dBm, you are looking at a specific amount of power; for instance, 0 dBm is exactly 1 mW, and 30 dBm is 1 watt. It tells you exactly how much energy is present in the signal at a given point.

dB, conversely, is not a measure of power on its own but represents the ratio between two values. It is used to describe gain or loss. If a component has a 3 dB gain, it has increased the signal power by a factor of two, regardless of the starting power. Essentially, dBm is like a specific temperature reading, whereas dB is like saying the temperature rose by five degrees.

question:
My understanding of Pulse Doppler Radar is the system measures Time Of Flight for the pulse.

My confusion is that during the down conversion process prior to ADC the lowpass filter causes some time delay in addition to the time of flight. In principle the delay should be known beforehand but I'm sure it's not exact and in general the delay is not completely constant even among the band of interest.

How is this delay dealt with?
answer_raw:
In most radar systems, the group delay introduced by the lowpass filter is negligible compared to the time of flight for the distances being measured. You're typically dealing with nanoseconds of delay versus microseconds or milliseconds for the target. Furthermore, designers use linear-phase filters to ensure that the delay remains constant across the signal's bandwidth, which prevents pulse distortion.

If you are working with ultra-high precision, this delay isn't solved in real-time; it's handled through system calibration. During a calibration phase, the system measures the total internal loop delay—often using a known internal reference or a fixed target—and subtracts this constant offset from the final range calculation. Because the hardware components are stable, once you've calibrated the "zero point" of the system, any remaining variations across the bandwidth are generally below the noise floor or the resolution limit of the range bins.

question:
I want to construct a reference locked sine oscillator. The multibit sine wave is calculated using DDS. The multibit reference signal is typically not sinusoidal, can have offset and substantial noise, but is expected to contain one dominant frequency.

If this dominant frequency is nearly known, a standard PLL approach will work to keep track of the dominant frequency in the reference signal.

However, I now suppose this cannot work to acquire initial reference lock if the dominant frequency is far away from the oscillator frequency. In this case, the PLL gets stuck on a locally dominant frequency.

What is the common approach to resolve this ? Calculating an DFT seems like overkill, since it produces a lot of unnecessary information. A recursive 4 sample Zoom FFT looks a bit more efficient. But maybe there is a way that directly modifies the PLL filter to capture further off frequencies ?

Please let me know if I missed crucial info.
answer_raw:
To handle wide frequency offsets, the standard approach is to implement a hybrid architecture combining a Frequency-Locked Loop (FLL) with your PLL. While a PLL is excellent for fine phase tracking, its capture range is naturally narrow. An FLL uses a frequency discriminator—such as a zero-crossing detector or a coarse frequency estimator—to provide a frequency error signal that is linear over a much broader range. This effectively pulls the oscillator toward the dominant frequency regardless of the initial phase ambiguity.

If you need more precision than a zero-crossing detector but want to avoid the overhead of a full DFT, the Goertzel algorithm is a great choice. It allows you to efficiently evaluate the power of a few specific candidate frequencies. Once the FLL or Goertzel search brings the oscillator within the PLL's pull-in range, you hand over control to the PLL for stable, low-jitter locking. This coarse-to-fine transition is the standard way to ensure wide-range acquisition.
